# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **Three million in Kyiv could lose heat, water and sanitation under Russia's winter strikes.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) Winter strikes hit the systems that keep Ukrainian cities running
**What happened (neutral):** The New York Times reported that Russia has opened an intense bombing campaign, weeks earlier than expected, against the infrastructure that keeps people alive through winter, and that daily strikes on the energy system have raised fears Kyiv, a city of three million, could become all but uninhabitable in the coming months. American-led talks resumed last week in Abu Dhabi after a nine-month lull, and in those talks Russia set out hard-line demands that stood little chance of acceptance by Ukraine and its European allies.

**Context & perspectives:** President Volodymyr Zelensky said after a recent attack, "They want to come to the table holding our energy system hostage." The Times reported that this unbending line indicated Moscow had no real interest in discussing peace now, because it believes the winter campaign will strengthen its negotiating position entering the spring. Knocking out power each winter has become Moscow's route to aims it has not achieved in nearly five years of war; cities are in their most precarious position yet because the grid is more fragile after years of strikes and air defenses are dwindling. A meeting on Thursday among President Trump, President Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping in Shenzhen left it unclear whether the three would discuss the war.

**Read more (sources):**
- [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world/europe/russia-ukraine-winter-campaign.html) — Winter infrastructure campaign and the Abu Dhabi talks

## Major world stories (3)
### 2) Ahmad Tibi elected a deputy speaker of Israel's Knesset
**What happened (neutral):** Al Jazeera reported that Ahmad Tibi, chairman of the Joint List, an alliance of parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, was elected on Monday by fellow members as a deputy speaker of the Knesset, Israel's parliament. Tibi, leader of the Ta'al party inside that alliance, told Al Jazeera the post was "a rightful achievement for the Joint List, which secured 11 seats" in the October 27 elections. Parties representing Palestinian citizens — the Joint List and the United Arab List, known as Ra'am — together hold 19 seats in the 120-member house, and the bloc endorsed Gadi Eisenkot after President Isaac Herzog tasked him this month with forming the next government.

**Context & perspectives:** Tibi said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir "attempted to prevent my election, but they failed despite their reckless incitement," and that the Joint List will be represented in all committees. On Sunday he called for a criminal investigation into Netanyahu and his aides. Israel's Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu's chief of staff, Ido Norden, contacted the police commissioner's office before the elections, alleging that three Ra'am activists in southern Israel carried large sums of cash and vouchers meant to sway voters; police relied on a former employee of the prime minister's office and arrested the activists after raids without valid search or arrest warrants. Tibi wrote on X, "No one is above the law, not even Netanyahu." He first entered the Knesset in 1999 and was a deputy speaker from 2006 to 2022.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/16/ahmed-tibi-appointed-as-deputy-speaker-of-israels-knesset?traffic_source=rss) — Tibi's election, the seat count, and the Channel 12 allegations

### 3) Ecuador's president says US troops are not a base
**What happened (neutral):** Al Jazeera reported that President Daniel Noboa denied on Sunday that the United States has a military base near the port city of Guayaquil, after voters rejected a referendum that would have allowed foreign military sites. The AFP news agency last month documented an unusual deployment of US aircraft at Taura Air Base, dozens of tents and infrastructure work, identified about 20 US military flights there from June to mid-October, and obtained documents referring to US soldiers.

**Context & perspectives:** The then-air force commander, General Mauricio Salazar, asked the armed forces in a September letter to clarify whether the deployment was legal, AFP said; he was later removed and reassigned to less senior duties. Quito and Washington have been deepening cooperation against drug trafficking. The Pentagon, its Southern Command and Ecuador's air force did not respond to requests for information when AFP published in October. Human Rights Watch has called the partnership "perilous," arguing that both governments have committed serious human rights violations fueled by framing confrontations with organized crime as a kind of war. Noboa had campaigned to reverse the constitutional ban on foreign bases; Ecuadorans voted against that change in a referendum in November last year.

CONTESTED: The dispute turns on what the tents, flights and documents at an Ecuadoran airfield amount to after voters kept the ban.
Noboa told the outlet Altavoz that US personnel are there only for "temporary activities," sometimes a specific mission or operation: "We work together. It's not an American base. It's an Ecuadoran base." His reason is operational partnership against regional drug trafficking, not a permanent foreign site. He did not address the aircraft AFP described, and he sidestepped a request to visit Taura.
Human Rights Watch's reason for calling the same partnership perilous is the war framing itself: equipment, training, intelligence and direct military support, paired with that framing, have gone along with serious human rights violations by both governments. The watchdog's limit is that it is judging the partnership, not publishing its own count of who is on the base. Senior Ecuadoran officers had already asked for a legal clarification, and the commander who asked was reassigned — a fact that sits beside Noboa's temporary-mission account without settling it.

**Questions to consider:**
- Will Quito or Washington publish the orders covering the US flights AFP counted at Taura from June to mid-October?

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/16/ecuadors-president-denies-us-has-military-base-in-country?traffic_source=rss) — Noboa's denial, AFP's documentation, and Human Rights Watch

### 4) Nigeria's president approves 28,000 more soldiers and 50,000 police
**What happened (neutral):** AllAfrica, citing Daily Trust, reported that the campaign council of the All Progressives Congress, President Bola Tinubu's party, said he has approved recruitment of 28,000 additional soldiers and 50,000 police officers to tackle insecurity across Nigeria.

**Context & perspectives:** The announcement is the council's account of a presidential approval, not a published timetable for when those recruits would be trained or deployed.

**Read more (sources):**
- [AllAfrica](https://allafrica.com/stories/202611160323.html) — Campaign council statement on the security recruitment

## Economy, science & technology (2)
### 5) WHO warns drug resistance could kill 39 million in 25 years
**What happened (neutral):** Al Jazeera reported that the World Health Organization, the United Nations health agency, warned on Monday that growing antimicrobial resistance — germs surviving the medicines meant to kill them — could cause 39 million deaths over the next 25 years and make routine surgery and childbirth life-threatening. In 2021 it was directly responsible for more than one million deaths and linked to about 4.7 million others. In 2023, one in six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections reported to the agency was resistant to the antibiotics used to treat it.

**Context & perspectives:** Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, acting director of the agency's antimicrobial-resistance department, said resistance is "threatening the future of modern medicine," and that unlike COVID-19 these infections "have been taking people's lives for years without us noticing." A review of 183 countries found nearly nine in 10 now have a national action plan, up from about four in 10 in 2017, but Pravasha Prakash, a technical officer, said only 42 countries — less than one in five — had a plan that was financed, implemented and monitored. Sylvia Bertagnolo, head of surveillance, said that without testing, clinicians must treat without knowing the cause or which antibiotic will work. The agency released two tools: one listing tests that should be available from primary care to referral hospitals, and one compiling 73 laboratory procedures from sample collection to identifying the germ and testing which drugs it resists. It named infection prevention, vaccination, water and sanitation, and careful use of these medicines as the main levers, and said progress is still too slow for 2030 targets.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/16/un-health-agency-sounds-alarm-on-antimicrobial-resistance-threat?traffic_source=rss) — Death estimates, country plans, and the new diagnostic tools

### 6) Lebanon sets December 14 for commercial flights at a second airport
**What happened (neutral):** Al Jazeera reported that Lebanon's second airport, Rene Mouawad in the northern town of Qlayaat, is scheduled to begin test flights on Independence Day, November 22, with commercial flights now expected on December 14, when many Lebanese living abroad come home for the winter holiday. Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and other officials took a test flight from Beirut in June. The airport had been aimed at mid-2026; Israel's war delayed it, and construction delays pushed commercial service from November 22 to mid-December.

**Context & perspectives:** Rafik Hariri International, just south of Beirut, is the country's only functioning airport and has been a political chokepoint: in February 2025, supporters of Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed Shia armed group, blocked the road to the capital when two Iranian planes were barred from landing. Inflation is expected to hit 17.5 percent this year, the World Bank predicts the economy will contract by 6.4 percent in 2026, and previous estimates put damage since 2023 at more than $14 billion. Recovery from the 2019 crash has been held back by Israel's assault and the US-Israel war on Iran.

CONTESTED: Everything turns on whether a small northern runway is an economic project or a political alternative to Beirut's single airport.
Lebanese officials say the reason is economic, not political: growth in one of the poorest, most underserved regions. That case rests on the north's lack of air links and on the holiday traffic the December 14 date is meant to catch.
Bassel Doueik, a political analyst, argues Hezbollah's ability to block the Beirut airport road is a strategic advantage whenever tensions with the government rise, and that Qlayaat decreases that advantage only somewhat because it is too small to replace Hariri. Marcel Baloukji, a political and security analyst, argues the state gains room to maneuver and a fallback if Beirut's airport is shut in a future war, especially for foreign nationals and diplomats, while conceding it does not change much for Hezbollah's arms or internal political calculations. Both analysts accept the airport cannot substitute for Hariri; they differ from the officials on whether that limited backup is still a political fact.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/11/16/lebanons-second-airport-could-provide-economic-and-political-benefits?traffic_source=rss) — Dates, the Beirut road block, and the economic figures

## Progress watch (1)
### 7) A rural Malawi hospital has electricity after a 48-hour promise
**What happened (neutral):** AllAfrica, citing Nyasa Times, reported that Local Government Minister Ben Phiri said Makanjira Rural Hospital now has electricity, as he had promised within 48 hours, and that he thanked the people who restored the power.

**Context & perspectives:** He blamed a commissioning mix-up for the outage that prompted the deadline. The report does not say how stable the restored supply is.

### Also Today
**Jordan bans Telegram app over 'radicalisation' claims: Deutsche Welle**
Jordan's Public Security Directorate banned the messaging app Telegram on Monday, after an October 23 shooting at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate that killed seven people and wounded 34, saying the ban is meant to block extremism that threatens national interests. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/jordan-bans-telegram-app-over-radicalisation-claims/a-79956706?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

**Nearly 2,200 migrants reach Canary Islands in 2 days, Spain says: AP News**
Spain said nearly 2,200 people reached the Canary Islands from Senegal in two days along the Atlantic route. Source: [apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/spain-migration-boat-rescue-canary-islands-c4aeb350f770567d571bbb5442299099)

**Russia out of IIHF World Junior Ice Hockey as Canada refuses entry: Al Jazeera**
The International Ice Hockey Federation said Russia's under-20 team cannot play the World Junior Championship, which will still run in Edmonton and Red Deer from December 26, 2026, to January 5, 2027, after Canada barred Russian and Belarusian athletes while the war in Ukraine continues, and Norway is back in the field. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11/16/russia-out-of-iihf-world-junior-ice-hockey-as-canada-refuses-entry?traffic_source=rss)

**France wants rare earths from Malaysia. What will it take to get them?: South China Morning Post**
President Emmanuel Macron, in Malaysia through Tuesday, wrote that he was coming in particular to diversify France's rare-earth supplies, while analysts said Malaysia's ability to supply them depends on processing bottlenecks that sustain China's dominance. Source: [scmp.com](https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics/article/3374606/france-wants-rare-earths-malaysia-what-will-it-take-get-them)

**USS Roosevelt arrives in Middle East: Is the US-Iran war about to resume?: Al Jazeera**
A US official told Al Jazeera the USS Theodore Roosevelt had arrived, a third US aircraft carrier in the region that the Pentagon has not formally confirmed, while President Trump called further strikes on Iran "quite unlikely" but said the military remains "locked and loaded." Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/16/uss-roosevelt-arrives-in-middle-east-is-the-us-iran-war-about-to-resume?traffic_source=rss)

China's Foreign Ministry said President Xi Jinping will host Presidents Trump and Putin in Shenzhen on November 19, calling it the first face-to-face meeting of the three heads of state, while US officials have indicated an agenda of Ukraine, West Asia including energy supplies, and nuclear arms control. ## Understanding the Issue: How a promise to one ally can empty a promise to all
People often hear a nonaggression pact as extra safety for the country that signs it. Al Jazeera's account of leaked demands, obtained by The New York Times, The Economist and several Ukrainian outlets, shows a different mechanism: Russia wants the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, the alliance that treats an armed attack on one member as an attack on all 32, to pull troops out of Central and Eastern Europe and to stop expanding. Negotiator Alexey Drobinin said agreements could be reached with individual member states, which would then receive additional security guarantees from Moscow. Former Russian diplomat Boris Bondarev, who quit the foreign ministry over the 2022 invasion, told Al Jazeera that a string of such deals would leave each European country face to face with Russia, and that the pacts would most likely bar a signatory from joining a later conflict between Russia and another European nation. That bar is the hinge: collective defense works only if allies may still fight when one of them is attacked. The demands were put to US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, not to European leaders. Maria Kucherenko of Kyiv's Strategic Intelligence Institute told Al Jazeera that Moscow prefers to talk to Washington, keeps demands maximalist, and puts politics ahead of security. Reading a communiqué, check whether any "individual guarantee" still lets that country fight if a neighbor in the same alliance is attacked. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/16/nato-will-collapse-russia-stalls-ukraine-talks-seeks-to-divide-europe?traffic_source=rss)

## Media-literacy note
When two outlets describe the same talks, read the demand each one actually quotes before you accept a summary of "hard line" or "breakthrough." A rights group, a campaign council and a ministry are not the same kind of source: the first investigates, the second advocates, the third governs. Primary documents — a court charge sheet, a referendum text, a surveillance table — settle more arguments than a second headline on the same event.

# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **Six drones targeted a US base in Bahrain, ending two months of calm.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) Strikes return over Bahrain after a two-month lull
**What happened (neutral):** Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps — a branch of Iran’s armed forces — said it launched six drones at a United States air-defence radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain, France 24 reported, in the second claimed strike on the Gulf kingdom in three days. Bahrain’s military said its air defences intercepted several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets, CNBC reported, and the foreign ministry said the systems shot down Iranian drones. There was no immediate confirmation from US or Bahraini authorities that the radar was hit. Sirens sounded, the first warnings since September, and blasts were reported around 4 a.m. local time and again around 6:30 a.m. Bahrain, home to the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet — the American naval command for the Gulf — told residents to stay calm and go to the nearest safe place. The interior ministry posted that guidance after two threat warnings.

**Context & perspectives:** The Guardian, in a live report, quoted Hayat Ibrahim, 65, telling Agence France-Presse that the blasts were what she had hoped would not return after the quiet. Two days earlier the Guards said they had hit a US early-warning radar in Bahrain; US Central Command, which runs American military operations in the region, said it had shot down two Iranian drones with no casualties or damage. CNBC reported that President Donald Trump has said in recent days he might hold off further attacks on Iran if there are no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, while keeping a US naval blockade. The same report said the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis intercepted two Houthi ballistic missiles launched toward Riyadh and three drones in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province. France 24 carried the Guards’ further line that the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow oil route at the mouth of the Gulf — “is closed,” and that any American aggression would meet a harsher response. Bahrain’s foreign ministry said the kingdom rejects having its territory used as an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible.

The attacks are contested in what they achieved and what they justify. The Guards’ stated case is retaliation for what they call hostile US actions, with a warning that further American force will be answered more heavily, and with the Hormuz claim attached to that same statement. Bahrain’s stated case is that the weapons were stopped short of their targets, that the pattern is a systematic hostile approach, and that Iran, not Bahrain, owns the consequences of firing at a kingdom that hosts a US fleet.

**Questions to consider:**
- Do US or Bahraini authorities later confirm any damage at Al-Riffa, or only interceptions?

**Read more (sources):**
- [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/bahrain-iran-drone-attacks-tehran-us-base.html) — Bahrain says it intercepted the attacks; Trump’s hold-off condition and the Houthi intercepts
- [France 24](https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/20261115-iran-claims-attack-on-us-military-airbase-in-bahrain) — Guards’ six-drone claim, the Hormuz line, and Bahrain’s responsibility statement
- [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2026/nov/15/middle-east-crisis-live-iran-bahrain-strikes-gulf-donald-trump-us-israel-yemen-houthis) — resident account of blasts after two months of calm
- [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/saudi-led-coalition-intercepts-missiles-towards-riyadh-drones-eastern-province-2026-11-15/) — coalition intercepts toward Riyadh and in the Eastern Province

## Major world stories (3)
### 1) Cape Verde votes, with a woman on the presidential ballot for the first time
**What happened (neutral):** Voters began casting ballots in Cape Verde, where President Jose Maria Neves faces five opponents, including Joana Rosa, the first woman to run for president since independence in 1975, Al Jazeera reported. More than 300,000 people are eligible, from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. local time, in a country often cited for stability in a volatile region. A winner needs more than 50 percent; otherwise the top two meet in a runoff on November 29. Results are expected within two to three days.

**Context & perspectives:** Neves, of the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde, the country’s oldest party, was prime minister for 15 years and became president in 2021. His party won 37 of 72 parliamentary seats in May, and he appointed Francisco Carvalho, then mayor of the capital, Praia, as prime minister. Rosa, of the Movement for Democracy and a former justice minister, comes from a party that governed for 10 years before that May vote. The presidency in this hybrid system has veto power and a mediating role, not day-to-day control of government. The islands have about 500,000 residents and more citizens abroad than at home, mostly in Portugal and the United States; nearly 77,000 diaspora voters are registered at embassies. The vote turns on emigration and scarce jobs. Roselma Evora, a professor of political science and gender studies at the University of Cabo Verde, told the Associated Press that many voters feel distant from a political class they think does not understand daily difficulties.

Rosa’s case is that government should let young people build a future on the islands and stop the exodus. Neves’s case is a second term built around a youth summit aimed at the same emigration problem. Each treats leaving as the crisis; they differ on whether the answer is a summit under the incumbent or a change of who holds the presidency.

**Questions to consider:**
- Does anyone clear 50 percent in the count expected within two to three days, or is the November 29 runoff on?

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/15/polls-open-in-cape-verde-in-race-with-first-female-presidential-candidate?traffic_source=rss) — candidates, rules, diaspora vote, and the emigration promises

### 2) ASEAN opens in Manila with energy shortages on the table
**What happened (neutral):** Leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations — an 11-country bloc that wants a single market but cannot impose decisions on members — opened their summit in Manila, running November 15 to 17, Al Jazeera reported. The bloc counts nearly 694 million people, about 8.4 percent of the world. Protesters met arriving leaders over the cost of basic goods and over Pax Silica, a US-led artificial-intelligence supply-chain initiative, Al Jazeera’s Barnaby Lo reported.

**Context & perspectives:** Oil and gas shortages tied to the US-Israel war on Iran are the energy issue import-dependent members brought into the room. The Philippines, Vietnam, and Malaysia are described as among the most exposed; Manila declared a national energy emergency in March. Millions of the bloc’s citizens live and work in the Middle East. Governments also worry the conflict could reach the Strait of Malacca, the narrow sea lane between Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore. US tariff increases of 10 to 12.5 percent since President Donald Trump’s second term have pushed the bloc to trade more with others. Trump is expected at a special meeting with members on November 17, then at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering in China on November 18–19. Other guests named by Al Jazeera include India’s Narendra Modi, Canada’s Mark Carney, Brazil’s Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva — the first sitting Brazilian president to visit the Philippines — and Russia’s foreign minister Sergey Lavrov. On the South China Sea, China and four members — Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam — plus Taiwan have long disputed a waterway believed to hold undersea oil and gas. A “code of conduct” negotiated since 2005 was meant, under a 2023 pledge, to reach a finished draft this year; at least 10 rounds were held this year, the last in October, led by Malaysia.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/15/asean-summit-whos-attending-and-whats-at-stake?traffic_source=rss) — energy, tariffs, guests, and the sea-code talks
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/video/newsfeed/2026/11/15/protesters-condemn-us-policies-as-asean-summit-begins-in-manila?traffic_source=rss) — protests over prices and Pax Silica
- [AP News](https://apnews.com/article/asean-summit-manila-philippines-china-trump-ca9bb47cc109a1ca9e57be787b137095) — summit opening with conflicts on the agenda

### 3) Portuguese cities march over rents
**What happened (neutral):** People marched in cities across Portugal against surging home prices, demanding government action on housing, Al Jazeera reported, while the Associated Press described the crowds as tens of thousands. Al Jazeera’s count was thousands. Authorities have begun changes aimed at lowering prices. Protesters told Al Jazeera that those steps are not enough.

**Context & perspectives:** The two counts are the outlets’ own: the Associated Press headline says tens of thousands; Al Jazeera says thousands. Neither report in the material names a new law, a rent figure, or a date for the next government step.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Associated Press](https://apnews.com/article/portugal-housing-protest-9605c8504a2e25b9f36266dd43ddcb23) — tens of thousands in Portuguese cities
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/video/newsfeed/2026/11/15/thousands-in-portugal-protest-against-surging-rental-prices?traffic_source=rss) — protesters say price-cutting steps fall short

## Economy, science & technology (2)
### 1) Commerce secretary presses for looser rules on chips used outside China
**What happened (neutral):** Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has pushed a less strict version of controls on sales of advanced artificial-intelligence chips to data centers outside China that still serve Chinese firms, The New York Times reported. In southern Malaysia, a center known as A201 is set to open next year with hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia’s most advanced servers, and plans to supply that computing to a Chinese tech giant. The Times said the setup is legal and sidesteps a US ban on selling the most advanced chips directly to Chinese firms. The operator is a client of Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm Lutnick formerly led and then handed to his sons. He is now writing rules that would substantially affect that business.

**Context & perspectives:** The Trump administration bans cutting-edge chip sales to China and has debated for much of the past two years how far to limit sales to Southeast Asian data centers. Both the ban on direct sales and the legality of a third-country center, as the Times describes them, sit under the argument. China hawks in that debate treat centers like A201 as a way for Beijing to get around the ban. Lutnick’s push is against limits that would cut Nvidia’s Asian sales by giving Washington more oversight of chips going to international data centers. The Times said that softer line has drawn criticism from lawmakers and others in the administration. The article does not name a date for a final rule.

**Read more (sources):**
- [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/politics/lutnick-pushed-to-weaken-chip-rules-that-overlap-with-his-family-business.html) — A201, Cantor Fitzgerald, and the split over Southeast Asian controls

### 2) South Korea’s top tax-exam scorer admits using AI
**What happened (neutral):** The top scorer on South Korea’s national exam for aspiring tax accountants confessed to using generative artificial intelligence to cheat, The Guardian reported. He had seemed too strong to be real: one wrong answer out of 160 questions across two exams, in April and July. The admission landed on Sunday. Organisers of the national college entrance exam this Thursday now face higher stakes, the same report said.

**Context & perspectives:** The Guardian said the scandal followed months of speculation about those near-perfect marks. It did not describe a penalty already imposed.

**Read more (sources):**
- [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/15/ai-cheating-south-korea-college-entrance-exam) — the confession and the Thursday college exam

## Progress watch (1)
### 1) Starship is caught by the launch tower
**What happened (neutral):** SpaceX recaptured its Starship rocket after a return from orbit, a first, the Associated Press reported, with the vehicle caught by arms on the launch pad. France 24 said the catch came after the booster was not caught the day before. Smaller earlier models have landed again, France 24 noted, but they need heavy legs and are not fully reusable.

**Context & perspectives:** The new fact is the catch itself, not another plan to try. The articles do not give a landing-site name, a crew, or a next flight date.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Associated Press](https://apnews.com/article/spacex-elon-musk-starship-rocket-df394c1b5a0f85e11194f9ff7db9ee6b) — first capture by launch-pad arms after a return from orbit
- [France 24](https://www.france24.com/en/spacex-makes-rocketry-history-by-recapturing-massive-reusable-rocketship) — the miss a day earlier, and why smaller rockets are not fully reusable

### Also Today
**Iraq PM sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran stronghold: Al Jazeera**
Iraq’s prime minister dismissed nine officials after a probe found illegal oil refineries and smuggling in a region run by Kataib Hezbollah, an Iran-aligned armed group. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/15/iraq-pm-sacks-nine-officials-over-oil-smuggling-in-pro-iran-stronghold?traffic_source=rss)

**Midterm voters ended the long-running GOP dominance in state legislatures: NPR**
Democrats took control of state legislatures that had been split and weakened Republican dominance in others, with health-care access and new limits on school vouchers on the agenda. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-6039175/midterms-legislatures-states-democrats-gop)

**Democrat Kreiss-Tomkins says his successful gubernatorial campaign covered every corner of Alaska: AP News**
Democrat Kreiss-Tomkins won Alaska’s governor’s race. Source: [apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/alaska-governor-democrat-kreiss-tomkins-9df98d3136219afede6d47ba7d15e5f7)

**China calls for AI cooperation with the US ahead of Shenzhen Apec summit: South China Morning Post**
Chinese ambassador to the United States Xie Feng called for major-power cooperation on artificial intelligence at this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen. Source: [scmp.com](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3374484/china-calls-ai-cooperation-us-ahead-shenzhen-apec-summit)

**De la Fuente denies racism in Spain despite Yamal, Vinicius avowals: Al Jazeera**
Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said there is no racism in Spain, after Lamine Yamal said he had faced it “a thousand times,” ahead of a Nations League match with England. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11/15/de-la-fuente-denies-racism-in-spain-despite-yamal-vinicius-avowals?traffic_source=rss)

**Netanyahu sends plea to Eisenkot for unity government: Al Jazeera**
Benjamin Netanyahu publicly asked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a unity government. Source: [aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/video/newsfeed/2026/11/15/netanyahu-sends-plea-to-eisenkot-for-unity-government?traffic_source=rss)

**At the Supreme Court, Trump aims to cut the power of judges again: Reuters**
President Donald Trump is asking the US Supreme Court, again, to narrow what judges can do. Source: [reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/supreme-court-trump-aims-cut-power-judges-again-2026-11-14/)

**Troubled Scottish steel supplier raises questions over Royal Navy contracts: The Guardian**
Liberty Steel’s Dalzell mill in Motherwell, with an order for 34,000 tonnes of plate for three Royal Navy warships, has struggled to pay bills and workers. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/15/liberty-steel-dalzell-scotland-royal-navy-contracts-warships)

**Digital finance products used to abuse almost 20% of young women and girls, UK report finds: The Guardian**
A Surviving Economic Abuse survey found almost one in five young women and girls in the UK had seen banking apps, online payments, or digital credit used by a partner as a tool of abuse. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026/nov/15/digital-finance-products-abuse-against-young-women-and-girls-report)

**Evolutionary threat: Chinese mountain birds lost nearly half genetic diversity in 50 years: South China Morning Post**
Scientists found that common songbirds in China’s mountains lost nearly half their genetic diversity over 50 years, the variation that lets a population adapt when threats change. Source: [scmp.com](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/article/3374287/evolutionary-threat-chinese-mountain-birds-lost-nearly-half-genetic-diversity-50-years)

**Thousands march in Rome to draw attention to the effects of the climate crisis: AP News**
Thousands marched in Rome calling attention to the effects of the climate crisis. Source: [apnews.com](https://apnews.com/video/thousands-march-in-rome-to-draw-attention-to-the-effects-of-the-climate-crisis-e56a97b6d5db4c0197ddcea2e033ef14)

## Understanding the Issue: How a chip ban can miss the customer who rents the computer
A common mix-up is to treat a chip ban as a ban on the work the chip can do. This explanation is the host’s own, not a finding from one of today’s articles. Export rules of this kind usually attach to a sale: who may buy the physical processor, and which destination that box may be shipped to. A data center in a country that is allowed to buy the chips can still rent the computing — the hours of calculation — to a customer in a country that is not allowed to buy the chips. The processor stays where it was legally sold. The data and the answers move. People who want a tight ban argue that the customer of the computing is the real end user, so oversight has to follow the service contract, not only the shipping label. People who want a narrower rule argue that once a sale is legal in the country where the machines sit, policing every later user of the service reaches past the chip and into ordinary cloud business. Reading coverage of any new control, the useful check is whether the draft limits the buyer of the hardware or also the customer who pays for the computing time.

## Media-literacy note
When two governments describe the same night, put each claim next to what was independently confirmed — interceptions, damage, or neither. A live quote from a resident is evidence of what that person heard, not of what a radar did. For a rule fight, read who would gain or lose money if the looser text wins, then read the security argument on its own terms. Primary statements — a military release, a court order, an election commission count — beat a headline that has already chosen a verb.

**Go deeper:** France 24 carries the Guards’ claim that the Strait of Hormuz is closed; CNBC reports Trump may hold off further strikes if Tehran and the Houthis offer no new provocations, while keeping a naval blockade.

# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **Russia holds a fifth of Ukraine, and Washington floated trading Donbas for NATO.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) Washington floats a Donbas withdrawal in exchange for NATO
**What happened (neutral):** Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday that American negotiators asked, for the first time, whether Ukraine would pull its remaining forces out of the eastern Donbas if it could join the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, or NATO, the BBC reports. He said he would send a package to a referendum only if it included security guarantees, no limits on Ukraine's army, and money to rebuild. The BBC reports that envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met him in Dublin on Thursday after talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow the day before, and that Russia occupies roughly a fifth of Ukraine, including most of Donetsk and Luhansk. US officials had previously said NATO membership was off the table; Zelensky said the question made him think "Nato is back on the agenda," while calling talks with Putin "an extremely difficult conversation."

**Context & perspectives:** Kyiv has long wanted alliance membership as the deterrent inside any deal, and Zelensky has refused to give up sovereign land even as Moscow demands the Donbas. Moscow's stated terms have included limits on the size of Ukraine's forces, territorial concessions, and guaranteed neutrality; Ukraine has rejected those as leaving it unable to stop another invasion. Kremlin comments, the BBC reports, suggest that position has not moved. France 24, citing remarks released by Zelensky's office, places the same American question after the latest round of talks in Abu Dhabi rather than after the Dublin meeting, and quotes him warning that the Kremlin's bid to rewrite Europe's security setup "lead[s] to wars or escalations" and that "Real security in Europe means the EU and NATO." The BBC adds that ceding the sliver Ukraine still holds in the Donbas would be small on the map and large as a symbol, because it would accept the Donbas as Russian, and that First Lady Melania Trump last month helped broker a temporary ceasefire in occupied Oleshky for evacuations and aid.

**Contested:** Zelensky's case is that a deal without guarantees, an unconstrained army, and rebuild funds is not a peace he can even ask voters to weigh, because membership is what would deter the next attack, and he is not willing to retreat from territory on a question alone. The Kremlin's case, as Putin and Russian officials have stated it, is that another NATO state on Russia's border is unacceptable, and that neutrality plus a smaller Ukrainian force is the condition that removes the threat Moscow says it is fighting. Zelensky himself flags the limit on his reading: Putin's signals make the conversation extremely hard. The articles do not record Moscow conceding any of its terms.

**Questions to consider:** If a written package with guarantees, no army cap, and rebuild funds appears, does Zelensky put it to a referendum?

**Read more (sources):**
- [BBC](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvg2l312ylqo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss) — Zelensky on the Donbas-for-NATO question, Dublin and Moscow meetings, and prior US position
- [France 24](https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261114-us-negotiators-suggest-ukraine-cedes-territory-in-exchange-for-nato-membership) — Same question, placed after Abu Dhabi talks, plus his EU-and-NATO security warning

## Major world stories (3)
### 1) US airspace halted after aging communications overloaded
**What happened (neutral):** The Federal Aviation Administration, the US agency that runs civil airspace, issued a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday after aging radar and telecom links controllers use between facilities began to falter at 3:36 p.m., The New York Times reports. France 24 reports that more than 8,200 flights, over 31 percent of those scheduled in the United States, were canceled, that the stop lasted nearly five hours, and that it was the longest in the country since September 11, 2001. Officials blamed outdated equipment and overloaded routers. The stop has been lifted and flights have resumed, though Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said recovery would take time and that he expected schedules back to normal by the Thanksgiving travel rush.

**Context & perspectives:** The Times reports this was only the third nationwide ground stop the agency has issued this century, and the second-longest after September 11, 2001; a shorter one followed a pilot-alert outage on January 11, 2023. More than 1,000 aircraft were airborne and bound for US airports during the stop. On a typical day more than 2 million people pass airport security; on Thursday the Transportation Security Administration screened nearly 2.5 million. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was never an indication of a cyberattack and that lives were never in danger, while adding that investigators were still looking and would not rule an attack out. France 24 reports officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. Duffy said last year Congress approved 12.5 billion dollars to upgrade facilities and technology, which he has called a down payment, and on Friday night he asked for another 50 billion dollars in emergency funding before the end of the year, up from a previous 30 billion dollar request, after which he said control of Congress and the budget switches from Republicans to Democrats.

**Contested:** Duffy's argument is that the same antiquated links will fail again unless Congress treats modernization as an emergency and delivers the larger sum while Republicans still hold the budget. Some Democratic lawmakers, the Times reports, have already asked whether the agency has spent the money it has been given efficiently and effectively — a check on writing another emergency cheque before that record is clear. The articles do not quote those lawmakers conceding that the current kit is adequate.

**Questions to consider:** Does Congress approve emergency air-traffic funding before control of the budget switches at the end of the year?

**Read more (sources):**
- [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/13/us/ground-stop-nationwide-flights-faa/nationwide-ground-stop-flights-faa) — Timing of the failure, Duffy's funding ask, and Mullin's cyber caveat
- [France 24](https://www.france24.com/en/us-nationwide-flight-ground-stop-our-routers-got-overloaded-with-data) — Cancellation count, duration, and the comparison with 2001

### 2) Sudan's aid plan is less than half funded
**What happened (neutral):** The International Organization for Migration and the UN refugee agency say funding gaps have run down emergency shelter and basic household goods for Sudan, Deutsche Welle reports. The United Nations plan needs 2.9 billion dollars to reach 20.4 million people; 47 percent has been raised. A total of 33.7 million people in the country depend on humanitarian aid. Some 15.4 million need emergency shelter and household items, and lack of money has let agencies assist only 10 percent of them.

**Context & perspectives:** More than three and a half years after fighting began between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, about 8.6 million people have fled inside the country, more than 4.6 million have left for neighbouring states, and another 5.2 million have gone back to ruined towns anyway. Death estimates run from 40,000 to 250,000; updated counts are unavailable while fighting, curbed satellite internet, and the exit of many observers continue. Marina Peter, chair of the Sudan and South Sudan Forum in Germany, told DW that some people have survived on roots, that food rations in refugee camps have been cut, and that child mortality is above average while the warring parties still block access. Ivo Körner of Caritas International told DW that the United States, Germany, and the European Union are giving far less than four or five years ago. Caritas still supports refugees and host communities with cash, drinking water, basic medical care, and seeds, but its 2026 Sudan projects have been financed only by donations. On October 23 the United Kingdom and 31 other partners, including Germany, said 19.5 million people — about 41 percent of the population — face acute food insecurity. Körner said he hopes for German Foreign Office money and expects opportunities to be tighter than in earlier years.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/sudan-misery-worsens-amid-plummeting-aid-for-displaced-people/a-79938864?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Funding gap, displacement counts, and aid groups' warnings

### 3) France's Saturday marches turn on pensions and policing
**What happened (neutral):** Campaign groups, students, and Yellow Vest protesters are due to march together in Paris this Saturday — a fifth straight Saturday — joining demands on wages, education, and civil liberties, France 24 reports. The Hindu reports that thousands of arrests, police beatings, and limits on marches have fed an anti-government swell that shows no sign of easing before next year's presidential election. The New York Times reports that the same weekend's demonstrations, and recent youth-driven protests in Belgium, Germany, Greece, Italy, and Portugal, sit on a budget fight: as people live longer, pensions are routinely the largest items in Europe's national budgets.

**Context & perspectives:** Union leaders, France 24 reports, warn that protest fatigue is setting in, while police officers are seeking better pay for the risk of policing the marches. France 24 also reports that many teachers back the students who have blockaded high schools for nearly two months, and that headteachers gathered on Friday saying threats and violence have become unbearable and asking the government to protect them.

**Contested:** Sébastien Ducros, a 36-year-old data analyst who supports the student protests, told the Times that dilapidated schools lose out because "a huge portion of the money is going toward retirees," and that people like his parents, about to retire, could give some pension back. Laurent Grinwald, 72, a retired postal worker, told the Times he is not eager to have his pension cut for other services after decades of work, especially with rents and the cost of living up. Jorge Galindo, director of the Spanish think tank EsadeEcPol, called it "a generational clash" and noted that Spain has some of Europe's most generous pensions. Neither Ducros nor Grinwald is quoted conceding the other's budget math.

**Read more (sources):**
- [France 24](https://www.france24.com/en/france-protests-for-fifth-saturday-against-living-costs-and-heavy-handed-policing) — Saturday's joint march and warnings of fatigue
- [The Hindu](https://www.thehindu.com/news/international/riots-in-france-how-anti-government-protests-spiralled-out-of-control/article71701195.ece) — Arrests, march limits, and the election backdrop
- [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world/europe/student-protests-pensions-generations.html) — Named split over whether pensions should yield

## Economy, science & technology (2)
### 1) The US loses its measles-elimination status
**What happened (neutral):** The Pan American Health Organization, the regional health body for the Americas, has revoked the United States' measles-elimination status after 26 years, Deutsche Welle reports, citing a Wall Street Journal account of people familiar with the decision. An independent commission of experts reporting to the organization's director concluded the country no longer qualified, a source close to the process told CNN. The test was whether one strain had spread without a break for 12 months or longer. A source familiar with the findings told Reuters the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found 12 months of continuous transmission. The agency has recorded 5,182 confirmed cases as of Thursday, across 45 states, New York City, and Washington, D.C. — more than double 2025's total of 2,289. About 7,500 people have been infected and 13 have died since 2025.

**Context & perspectives:** Nearly all of this year's cases are in people who were unvaccinated or whose status is unknown, and roughly one in nine patients were hospitalized, CNN reported, citing the CDC. Noel Brewer, a University of North Carolina professor who chairs an independent measles panel and who presented the CDC report to the regional body on Tuesday, told Reuters: "It is a fully preventable disease. It is unconscionable that we have this amount of measles." Johns Hopkins epidemiologist William Moss told Reuters the loss hurts the country's reputation as a public-health leader and means large outbreaks will continue. The period has coincided with greater vaccine hesitancy under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who for years has shown skepticism about measles-vaccine safety without scientific proof. CDC Director Erica Schwartz, before the decision, said the agency would keep working with states to encourage vaccination. To regain the status, a country must stop transmission and stay outbreak-free for at least 12 months.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/us-loses-measles-elimination-status-after-26-years-wsj-reports/a-79946974?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Status revocation, case counts, and the path back

### 2) Starship reaches orbit; the booster does not come home
**What happened (neutral):** SpaceX launched Starship, which it calls the world's largest spaceship, on a 15th test flight meant to put the craft in orbit and release 15 satellites for its Starlink network, France 24 reports. Deutsche Welle reports the company had planned, for the first time, to catch and later reuse both stages. The spacecraft continued into orbit. The booster, which was supposed to return to the pad, did not.

**Context & perspectives:** France 24 reports the booster splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico minutes after liftoff. Deutsche Welle reports the booster exploded over the Gulf of Mexico. Neither account publishes wreckage imagery or a company statement that would show which description the hardware supports; both agree the upper stage flew on and the booster was not recovered.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/spacex-launches-starship-rocket-fails-to-recover-booster/a-79946091?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Catch-and-reuse plan, and a report that the booster exploded
- [France 24](https://www.france24.com/en/spacex-s-starship-encounters-problems-during-15th-test-flight) — 15th flight, 15 satellites, and a splashdown account

## Progress watch (1)
### 1) Dakar closes the first Olympic event hosted in Africa
**What happened (neutral):** The Summer Youth Olympics in Dakar ended Friday after two weeks, the first time an African country has hosted an Olympic event, Deutsche Welle reports. Nearly 2,700 young athletes competed in 153 medal events across 25 sports, African nations took home a record medal haul, and Senegal won an Olympic gold for the first time, with 136 Senegalese athletes in the games. China led the gold table with 18, Japan took 11, Russia eight, Egypt six, and Ethiopia and Senegal five each.

**Context & perspectives:** International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry said expectations had been exceeded and that the games showed what can happen "when an entire country comes together for its young people." The complication is political: it was the first Olympic event since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 in which Russian athletes competed under their own flag. Chile, Paraguay, and Thailand have confirmed bids for the next Summer Youth Olympics, in 2030.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/senegal-youth-olympics-in-dakar-end-on-high-note/a-79944820?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Medal table, first African host, and Russia's flag

### Also Today

**Hong Kong to trial electronic proxy voting platform to curb bid-rigging at estates: South China Morning Post**

Source: [scmp.com](https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/society/article/3374434/hong-kong-trial-electronic-proxy-voting-platform-curb-bid-rigging-estates)

**Can Nvidia survive without tech titan Jensen Huang?: France 24**
The Financial Times, cited by France 24, says Nvidia has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a possible successor after Jensen Huang resigned. Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/can-nvidia-survive-without-tech-titan-jensen-huang)

## Understanding the Issue: How the worker-to-retiree ratio locks a national budget
A common picture of Europe's pension fights is that they are only a quarrel about whether older people have been too comfortable. The mechanism is a headcount. Germany's public pension insurance had 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957; by 2025 that ratio was 2.1, and by 2045 it is projected to fall to 1.73, which in headcount is 35.35 million contributors financing 16.82 million retirees, Deutsche Welle reports in a data check on the generations. To keep contribution rates from jumping with that shift, the pension system already receives about 118 billion euros a year in government subsidies, roughly a quarter of the federal budget, so a rising share of everyone else's taxes is already spoken for before schools, housing support, or training are debated. The same check finds the squeeze is not abstract: retirees on federal basic income support rose from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024, and low-income households' rent share rose from about 24 percent of income in 1990 to nearly 36 percent in 2021. In 2025, 11 percent of the population spent more than 40 percent of disposable income on housing, and among people at risk of poverty that figure was 35 percent. Public education spending on people under 30 has doubled since 2011, from about 4,000 euros to about 8,000 euros a person each year, yet in 2022 it was still 4.6 percent of gross domestic product against an OECD average of 4.7 percent — more money, a middle-of-the-pack share. Youth researcher Simon Schnetzer told DW the fair historical question is whether earlier generations had it hard too, and that young people are answering a different one: whether they have been given conditions to live, work, and keep the system funded. Read a street report against that ratio and that budget share, and the argument stops being "old versus young" and becomes "what is already committed before this year's argument starts." Next time a pension protest is covered, check whether the piece states the contributor-to-retiree ratio and the subsidy share, or only the crowd. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/gen-z-protests-do-baby-boomers-really-have-it-better-than-young-people/a-79918854?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

## Media-literacy note
When two outlets describe the same remark, write down the place each one attaches to it before you decide the diplomacy has moved. A status revoked by a regional health body is a decision; the case count underneath it is a separate document, and both deserve a look. Funding percentages and medal tables are checkable; a mood about a generation is not, until someone shows the ratio.

**Go deeper:** The BBC places the Donbas question after Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin, following Moscow, and notes Washington had taken NATO membership off the table; France 24 places that question after talks in Abu Dhabi and adds his line that only the EU and NATO are real European security.

# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **Global Microsoft outage disrupted services for millions of users over 12 hours.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) Microsoft outage disrupts global services including UK hospitals and police
**What happened (neutral):** Microsoft reported early signs of stabilisation after a global outage that affected Teams, Outlook and other services for more than 12 hours, with no indication of a cyber-attack, according to The Guardian. The company extended the email timeout window to 48 hours while recovery efforts continued. The outage hit UK hospitals, GPs, schools and police forces, causing delays in prescriptions and cancelled meetings.

**Context & perspectives:** Microsoft said a portion of its infrastructure experienced elevated load that likely contributed to connectivity errors, and some servers became unexpectedly unavailable during automated checks. The company warned that restarted services could become unresponsive again once traffic returned. The UK government said it was working closely with Microsoft to assess impact on services while maintaining contingency plans.

**Read more (sources):**
- [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage-outlook-teams-word-excel-reports) — detailed recovery timeline and UK service impacts
- [The Hindu International](https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/technology/microsoft-outage-live-updates-november-13-2026-steps-to-fix-outlook-and-other-apps-ongoing/article71696624.ece) — live updates on infrastructure load issues

## Major world stories (3)
### 2) Indonesia’s upper house to select new vice-president on December 2
**What happened (neutral):** Indonesia’s upper house of parliament will pick the country’s new vice-president on December 2 after the resignation of Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the president’s deputy and son of his predecessor, the South China Morning Post reported. Gibran’s resignation followed a month of political pressure after courts ruled on his eligibility.

**Context & perspectives:** The move could widen the gulf between President Prabowo Subianto and former president Joko Widodo. Analysts have noted the timing places the selection just weeks after the resignation.

**Read more (sources):**
- [South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast-asia/article/3374367/indonesias-upper-house-pick-new-vp-december-2) — timeline of the resignation and court rulings

### 3) Europe set to join next round of Ukraine-Russia peace talks
**What happened (neutral):** Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and US envoy Jared Kushner said Europe would join the next round of talks with Russia after US envoys held over four hours of discussions with Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin, France 24 reported. Putin indicated Moscow will not compromise on its hardline demands.

**Context & perspectives:**
**The strongest case for full European inclusion rests on the need to prevent Russia from diverting attention to broader security architecture questions and to ensure any outcome reflects European interests directly, as EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas argued that excluding Europe would leave the continent in a worse position.** Kallas stressed that the agreed sequence of ceasefire first, then peace agreement, must be maintained because Russia is presenting maximum demands. The counter-position holds that starting with European security architecture discussions risks weakening the focus on the aggressor-victim dynamic and allows Russia to exploit divisions, a view Kallas said would leave Europe worse off if pursued.

**Read more (sources):**
- [France24](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261113-big-development-in-peace-talks-as-ukraine-says-europe-to-join-russia-negotiations) — details of the Kremlin meeting and Zelensky statement
- [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2026/nov/13/eu-leaders-negotiations-ukraine-russia-dublin-ai-summit-kushner-witkoff-latest-news-updates) — Kallas comments on sequence and representation

### 4) Tanker carrying LNG hit mine and exploded in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says
**What happened (neutral):** Iran reported that a tanker carrying LNG hit a mine and suffered an explosion in the Strait of Hormuz, The Hindu International said. Tankers continue to face attacks in the strait despite a rebound in traffic and falling oil prices.

**Context & perspectives:** The incident occurs amid expectations of de-escalation in the US-Israeli conflict with Iran. Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein separately told France 24 that the “no war and no peace” situation cannot continue and confirmed Iraqi oil is now flowing through the strait under US protection.

**Read more (sources):**
- [The Hindu International](https://www.thehindu.com/news/international/tanker-carrying-lng-hit-mine-suffered-explosion-in-hormuz-iran/article71696996.ece) — details of the reported mine incident
- [France24](https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/t%C3%AAte-%C3%A0-t%C3%AAte/20261113-no-war-and-no-peace-between-the-us-and-iran-cannot-continue-iraqi-fm-says) — Iraqi foreign minister assessment of regional situation

## Economy, science & technology (2)
### 5) EU leaders hold first dedicated AI summit in Dublin
**What happened (neutral):** European Union leaders met in Dublin for the first ever summit on artificial intelligence, Deutsche Welle reported. European Council President Antonio Costa had written to leaders calling for discussion on opportunities and the technology’s transformative effect on economies and societies.

**Context & perspectives:** French AI company Mistral’s CEO Arthur Mensch and researcher Geoffrey Hinton are expected to speak. Estonia and Finland called for EU-level arrangements to respond to serious AI incidents, while Mistral urged Europe to push ahead rather than slow development.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/eu-leaders-gather-for-first-ever-ai-summit/a-79937463?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — summit agenda and participant letters

### 6) BMW begins major layoffs at its largest global production hub in China
**What happened (neutral):** BMW Brilliance, the joint venture in Shenyang where BMW holds a 75 per cent share, began cutting an estimated 1,800 to 2,000 jobs from November 2, the South China Morning Post reported. The move follows rivalry from Chinese carmakers.

**Context & perspectives:** The entire city felt the shock from the layoffs at the German carmaker’s largest production hub worldwide.

**Read more (sources):**
- [South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/economy/global-economy/article/3374366/chinese-carmaker-rivalry-sparks-bmw-layoffs-and-blowback-chinas-rust-belt) — scale of job cuts and local impact

## Progress watch (1)
### 7) Brazil Amazon deforestation falls 41 per cent to record low
**What happened (neutral):** Deforestation in Brazil’s Amazon decreased by 41 per cent between August 2025 and 2026 to reach its lowest rate since records began, according to data cited in coverage of the Tropical Forest Forever Facility. The drop marks measurable improvement in forest protection.

**Context & perspectives:** The reduction occurred while global deforestation trends continued elsewhere, with more than 8 million hectares lost worldwide in 2024 alone.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/is-the-tfff-rainforest-fund-failing-due-to-a-lack-of-money/a-79878673?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Brazil Amazon data and context

## Also Today
**Zimbabwe: Mnangagwa Clips Ally Tagwirei's Wings - Says He Can Only Administer Two Acts in New Ministerial Role: AllAfrica**
President Emmerson Mnangagwa has limited close ally Kudakwashe Tagwirei’s ministerial powers to administering only two acts, barely a month after elevating the businessman to cabinet. Source: [allafrica.com](https://allafrica.com/stories/202611130218.html)

**Toera's homecoming: Madagascar's slain king joins his ancestors after 129 years: France24**
France returned the skull of King Toera, killed by colonial troops in 1897, and the Sakalava people placed it among ancestors in their most sacred ritual for the first time since his death. Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261113-toera-s-homecoming-madagascar-s-slain-king-joins-his-ancestors-after-129-years)

**Amnesty criticises South Sudan, UN over failure to heed massacre warnings: France24**
Amnesty International said South Sudan and UN peacekeepers failed to act on warnings before a massacre that killed more than 200 people in March. Source: [france24.com](https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261113-amnesty-criticises-south-sudan-un-over-failure-to-heed-massacre-warnings)

**Germany news: Parliament agrees on debt-laden 2027 budget: Deutsche Welle**
The Bundestag budget committee approved a 2027 spending plan that includes the second-highest amount of new borrowing in modern German history, at just over €210 billion. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-parliament-agrees-on-debt-laden-2027-budget/live-79936897?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

**Czechia braces for massive protest against cuts to public media: Deutsche Welle**
Hundreds of thousands are expected in Prague to protest a fast-tracked bill that would replace the licence fee model for Czech Television and Czech Radio with direct state budget funding and cut budgets by around 15 per cent. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/czechia-braces-for-massive-protest-against-cuts-to-public-media/a-79933533?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

**After suffering its worst election result, what's next for the ANC — and for South Africa?: Deutsche Welle**
South Africa’s African National Congress secured under 31 per cent of the vote in local government elections, its worst result since 1994, prompting the party to schedule a special National Executive Committee meeting. Source: [dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/after-suffering-its-worst-election-result-what-s-next-for-the-anc-and-for-south-africa/a-79929902?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss)

## Understanding the Issue: How EU leaders coordinate on artificial intelligence policy
Many assume decisions on artificial intelligence rules in the European Union are made only by the European Commission without direct involvement from national heads of government. European Council President Antonio Costa wrote to leaders stating that a first dedicated discussion at leaders’ level is now needed because of the rapid pace of AI development. The summit took place in Dublin’s Convention Center, the same venue used for the European Political Community summit earlier in the week. French AI company Mistral’s CEO Arthur Mensch and Nobel-prize winner Geoffrey Hinton were scheduled to address the gathering. Estonia and Finland sent a letter ahead of the meeting calling for EU-level arrangements to respond to serious AI incidents while urging responsible governance. Mistral has argued against slowing development and pressed instead for Europe to advance its own capabilities. This direct leader-level format shows that national governments are engaging on both the economic opportunities and the risks of the technology, rather than leaving the file entirely to Brussels institutions. When reading future coverage, check which national letters or statements from heads of government are cited as shaping the summit outcomes.

## Media-literacy note
Cross-check claims about service disruptions against multiple company status pages and government statements rather than single social media posts. Primary documents such as the European Council president’s letter to leaders provide the clearest record of what was actually requested at the AI summit. Comparing the same event across outlets from different regions reveals which details each emphasises and which sources they quote directly.

# Omni View — Omni‑View Briefing
> **New speed limits on Ukraine's Starshield network are hindering drone interceptions as US envoys meet Putin to discuss ending the war.**

## Today's lead story (1)
### 1) US envoys meet Putin amid new Starshield restrictions in Ukraine
**What happened (neutral):** Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that military units recorded significant disruptions to Starshield operations across the entire front line and in occupied territories for several days. The restrictions set an effective speed limit of 161 kilometers per hour on terminals, disconnecting any moving faster, and these were described as systematic rather than random errors. US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin after trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi produced no major breakthrough on a ceasefire or territorial settlement; the envoys were later scheduled to meet Zelenskyy on the sidelines of a summit in Ireland.

**Context & perspectives:** CNBC and France24 present the speed caps as a concrete operational problem for Ukrainian interception of jet-powered drones, noting that similar limits appeared last month and that strikes have already succeeded because systems could not reach required speeds. BBC and Al Jazeera place the technical changes alongside the arrival of the US envoys in Moscow and the earlier Abu Dhabi meetings, underscoring Zelenskyy's request to clarify the circumstances directly with the American side. The reports share the undisputed technical detail that terminals above 161 kilometers per hour lose connection and that this affects drone defense; they diverge on whether the pattern reflects deliberate policy choices during active diplomacy or adjustments by the commercial operator.

The strongest case for viewing the restrictions as systematic policy holds that uniform speed thresholds applied consistently along the front line, combined with prior disputes over military use of the network, indicate coordinated limits rather than isolated faults, as Ukrainian documentation showed repeated disconnections at the same threshold. The strongest case for treating them as technical or negotiable holds that Starshield remains a system whose operators retain authority to set performance parameters during ongoing talks, with the possibility of full restoration once diplomatic progress occurs.

**Read more (sources):**
- [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/starlink-starshield-ukraine-restrictions-spacex.html) — Details on speed limits and military impact
- [BBC](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwrkgmymk55zo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss) — Envoys' arrival and meeting schedule
- [France24](https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261112-new-systematic-restrictions-starshield-network-kill-more-ukrainians-zelensky-says) — Zelenskyy's statement on systematic nature
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/12/us-envoys-arrive-in-moscow-for-russia-ukraine-talks-with-putin?traffic_source=rss) — Context of prior Abu Dhabi talks

## Major world stories (3)
### 2) Aid shortfalls slow Ebola response in DR Congo
**What happened (neutral):** Six months into the Ebola outbreak in Congo, Doctors Without Borders states that the virus continues to spread out of control and that large sums of international aid are not reaching frontline teams. The medical charity highlighted that response operations remain under-resourced in affected areas despite earlier pledges.

**Context & perspectives:** AllAfrica coverage centers on the charity's assessment that funding gaps leave treatment and containment teams without adequate supplies and personnel. The account focuses on the immediate operational consequences for containing the spread rather than assigning responsibility for the aid-flow problems.

**What happens next:** Health authorities will monitor whether pledged funds reach treatment centers in the coming weeks.

**Read more (sources):**
- [AllAfrica](https://allafrica.com/stories/202611120312.html) — MSF statement on aid delivery

### 3) Attack in northwest Pakistan kills ten police and 18 fighters
**What happened (neutral):** Fighters opened fire on police officers returning from a mine in Kohat district, killing ten officers and 18 attackers in the clash. Authorities described the incident as an ambush in a region with ongoing militancy.

**Context & perspectives:** Al Jazeera reports the event as a direct confrontation between security forces and armed groups, with the death toll reflecting the intensity of the exchange.

**What happens next:** Local authorities will investigate the circumstances of the ambush.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/12/ten-police-officers-18-fighters-killed-in-northwest-pakistan-attack?traffic_source=rss) — Details of the attack

### 4) Study finds widespread sexual harassment in German military
**What happened (neutral):** A Bundeswehr study found that sexual misconduct is far more widespread than previously recorded, with younger women affected at disproportionately higher rates. Defence Minister Boris Pistorius responded by calling for a policy of zero tolerance.

**Context & perspectives:** Deutsche Welle presents the findings as evidence that earlier internal assessments had understated the scale of the problem across the armed forces.

**What happens next:** The ministry will review implementation of the zero-tolerance measures.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/bundeswehr-study-exposes-widespread-sexual-harassment-in-german-military/a-79926359?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-xml-mrss) — Study results and ministerial response

## Economy, science & technology (2)
### 5) Hong Kong group issues guide on responsible AI use
**What happened (neutral):** The Artificial Intelligence Association of Hong Kong released a 209-page guide that calls on organizations to designate clear owners for AI initiatives to strengthen accountability as autonomous AI agents become more common. The document urges practical steps for corporate and institutional adoption of the technology.

**Context & perspectives:** South China Morning Post coverage presents the guide as an industry-led effort to establish concrete standards that address emerging risks in AI deployment across sectors.

**What happens next:** Companies will be encouraged to designate responsibility roles when deploying new AI systems.

**Read more (sources):**
- [South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/hong-kong-economy/article/3374227/cross-industry-association-hong-kong-releases-guide-responsible-ai-use) — Guide contents and launch

### 6) Public funds seen as key to owning AI-driven economic shifts
**What happened (neutral):** Reuters reports that public investment vehicles channeling capital into AI are positioned to capture the major economic trends driven by the technology. The analysis notes the growing role of these funds in shaping deployment and long-term growth areas.

**Context & perspectives:** The account focuses on the scale of public-fund involvement and its potential to influence which megatrends dominate future economic activity.

**Read more (sources):**
- [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/public-funds-ploughing-cash-into-ai-will-own-megatrends-shaping-economy-2026-11-12/) — Analysis of public investment role

## Progress watch (1)
### 7) UK appoints climate security envoy as island nations press for action
**What happened (neutral):** The United Kingdom named a climate security envoy while leaders of small island states described rising seas as a life-or-death issue at COP31 in Antalya. The appointment comes amid warnings from vulnerable nations about the pace of warming.

**Context & perspectives:** AP News frames the move as a diplomatic response to pressure from island leaders seeking stronger commitments on climate-related security risks.

**What happens next:** The envoy will coordinate UK positions on climate-related security risks in upcoming negotiations.

**Read more (sources):**
- [AP News](https://apnews.com/article/cop31-climate-targets-fail-islands-warming-f3e3326d07ab4fbff40c37b605ecd66c) — Appointment and island leaders' statements

## Also Today
**Nigeria demands release of detained journalist:** Amnesty International Nigeria and SERAP call for the release of Foundation for Investigative Journalism reporter Daniel Ojukwu, held over 2023 articles. Source: [allafrica.com](https://allafrica.com/stories/202611120294.html)

**South Korea urged to use economic ties with Laos against North Korean schemes:** Analysts recommend Seoul leverage growing influence in Laos to curb alleged IT worker scams funding Pyongyang's weapons programs. Source: [scmp.com](https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/article/3374220/how-south-korea-can-curb-pyongyangs-job-scams-laos-weapons-programmes)

## Understanding the Issue: How satellite speed limits affect frontline military operations
Most coverage of satellite service restrictions treats them as simple technical glitches, yet the Starshield case shows how performance parameters can directly shape battlefield outcomes. The network, built on Starlink technology for government and national-security use, allows operators to set speed thresholds that disconnect units exceeding those limits. In Ukraine's situation, the 161-kilometer-per-hour cap prevents systems on faster-moving platforms from maintaining connections, which in turn reduces the ability of interception units to match the speed of incoming jet-powered drones. This mechanism arises because commercial satellite constellations prioritize network stability and regulatory compliance over unrestricted military speeds. Knowing this, when reports mention "disruptions," readers can distinguish between random outages and deliberate parameter changes by checking whether the limits are uniform across regions and consistent over time. The same logic applies to any future claim about restored access: verify whether the speed threshold itself has been lifted rather than assuming connectivity equals full capability. One concrete check is to ask whether official statements specify the exact speed or altitude parameters still in force after any announced fix. Another useful step is to compare the technical description in operator updates against statements from military users on the ground to see whether the same numerical limit appears in both. This approach helps separate operational constraints from diplomatic signaling. Source: [cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/starlink-starshield-ukraine-restrictions-spacex.html)

## Media-literacy note
Cross-reference official statements from all parties involved in negotiations with technical details released by operators. Primary documents such as presidential social-media posts and company technical descriptions provide clearer grounding than secondary summaries.

**Go deeper:** [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/starlink-starshield-ukraine-restrictions-spacex.html) and [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/12/us-envoys-arrive-in-moscow-for-russia-ukraine-talks-with-putin?traffic_source=rss) both report the Starshield restrictions and envoy meetings from different regional vantage points.
